2.text: exactly fitting the rib (Fig. 17, a). A hole is drilled through the upper edge of the

3.text: slot on the inner side of the runner, and the line that fastens the rib passes

4.text: through that hole. All joints are fastened together with thin, pliant thongs,

5.text: which are drawn very tight, without any pegs or nails. The pack-sledge

6.text: (Fig. 17, b) is made of larch-wood, and is of rude workmanship. The fore-

7.text: ends of the rails are often straight, and tied to the runners in a very simple

8.text: way (Fig. 17, c). The runners are thick; but the ribs frequently break or

9.text: become unfastened under pressure. These sledges vary in size, according to

10.text: their special loads. Those carrying the halves of the outer tent-cover are the

11.text: largest; those for house utensils, kettles, etc., are supplied with a framework

12.text: open on one side (Fig. 17, d); and the smallest ones, on which the poles

13.text: are carried, often have a forked rail in the middle (Fig. 17, e). The tent-

14.text: poles are attached to the arms of this fork. The driving-sledge (Fig. 17, f)

15.text: is made of birch-wood, with thin, flat runners, curved ribs, and a frame of

16.text: flat, slender sticks tied together with thongs. Often a hoop is fastened in the

17.text: middle in an upright position, from which to suspend a bell. In the spring-

18.text: time, when the birch runners do not glide so smoothly over the half-melted

19.text: snow, they are shod with slabs of whalebone, or with several lengths of flat

20.text: pieces of bone cut from the whale’s jaw and joined together (Fig. 17, g).

21.text: This shoeing is fastened with thongs, which are sunk into grooves in order

22.text: to avoid friction against the snow, or simply with wooden pegs, or with a

23.text: combination of both. Driving-sledges are not ungraceful in shape; but they

24.text: are very brittle, and can be shivered to pieces by striking against any obstacle.

25.text: They vary in form and dimension. The woman’s sledge is usually larger than

26.text: others, and has a wider and more comfortable seat. The usual measurements

27.text: for the man’s driving-sledge are: length, 180-200 cm.; distance between the

28.text: runners, in the middle, 30-35 cm.; height in the middle, 24 cm. The measure-

29.text: ments for the woman’s driving-sledge are: length, 220-250 cm.; distance between

30.text: the runners, 35-40 cm.; height, 25 cm. The racing-sledge, on the contrary,

31.text: is so small, that the driver has hardly room to sit. Even the woman’s sledge

32.text: is so light, that a man can easily lift it with one hand and carry it on his

33.text: back, not to speak of drawing it with a rope over the snow. The seats of

34.text: driving-sledges, of whatever shape, are usually supplied with a low back.

35.text: A special sledge, larger and broader than any pack-sledge, has a square

36.text: frame (Fig. 18, a) covered with skin, and is used for carrying small children

37.text: when changing the abode in the cold season. The woman’s driving-sledge is

38.text: sometimes furnished with a small covered space on the back seat in which to

39.text: carry her infant (Fig. 18, b, c). The coverings are usually adorned with a

40.text: fringe of tassels, and are embroidered along the edges (see Plate XXI, Fig. 1).

41.text: A large circular piece of embroidery (see Plate XXI, Figs. 2-4), called “sun”

42.text: or “moon” according to its pattern, is also fastened on the back of the sledge.
